definition: Proactive learning is a generalization of active learning designed to relax unrealistic assumptions and thereby reach practical applications.
details: "In real life, it is possible and more general to have multiple sources of information with differing reliabilities or areas of expertise. Active learning also assumes that the single oracle is perfect, always providing a correct answer when requested. In reality, though, an "oracle" (if we generalize the term to mean any source of expert information) may be incorrect (fallible) with a probability that should be a function of the difficulty of the question. Moreover, an oracle may be reluctant – it may refuse to answer if it is too uncertain or too busy. Finally, active learning presumes the oracle is either free or charges uniform cost in label elicitation. Such an assumption is naive since cost is likely to be regulated by difficulty (amount of work required to formulate an answer) or other factors." Proactive learning relaxes all four of these assumptions, relying on a decision-theoretic approach to jointly select the optimal oracle and instance, by casting the problem as a utility optimization problem subject to a budget constraint.

explainer.lead: Proactive learning generalises active learning by dropping the assumption of a single, always-correct, always-willing source of labels. It matters because real labelling situations involve several imperfect and sometimes unavailable experts.

tiers.eli5: Instead of asking one all-knowing teacher every question, you ask several helpers who are sometimes wrong or too busy, and you decide who to ask what.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to choose which source to query when labels can come from multiple fallible annotators or sensors, weighing cost, reliability and difficulty. A common pitfall is failing to model how error probability grows with question difficulty, which leads to over-trusting experts on hard cases.
tiers.paperLevel: It relaxes active learning's single-perfect-oracle assumption to allow multiple information sources with differing reliabilities or expertise; an oracle may be incorrect with a probability that should depend on question difficulty, and may be reluctant to answer.

explainer.example: A model deciding between two annotators picks the cheaper one for easy questions and the more reliable one for hard questions, since the cheaper annotator's error rate rises with difficulty.
